name: Sivagurunathaswamy Temple, Sivapuram
deity: Shiva as Sivagurunathaswamy (Sivapuranathar), with the goddesses Aryambal and Singaravalli
tradition: Shaiva — a Paadal Petra Sthalam, sung in the Tevaram
summary: Sivapuram, a short way east of Kumbakonam, honours Shiva as Sivagurunathaswamy — also Sivapuranathar — a Paadal Petra Sthalam of the Kaveri country, with the goddesses Aryambal and Singaravalli. Its very name is explained by a tradition that countless Shiva lingams lie beneath its soil. Remembered as Kuberapuri, where Kubera regained his place among the gods, and as a place where Vishnu in his boar form worshipped the lord, the temple carries a layered lore beneath its quiet delta setting.

sections.history: Sivapuram, about six kilometres east of Kumbakonam, is an ancient Shaiva site revered in the Tevaram and counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams of the Chola country. The stone temple is of the Chola period with later additions. Its layered historical names — Kuberapuram, Bhookailas, Shenbagaranyam — and the tradition of a village resting over countless buried lingams give the place a reputation for deep and hidden sanctity.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the Dravidian plan with a gopuram, prakara and the sanctum of Sivagurunathaswamy. Uncommonly it has two goddess shrines, Aryambal and Singaravalli. The sthala vriksham is traditionally the shenbagam, the champak. The temple's reputation as 'Bhookailas' — Kailasa on earth — reflects the belief that the ground itself is dense with the presence of the lord.
sections.legends: Several stories gather at Sivapuram. Kubera, cursed by Nandi to be born on earth, came as the king Dhanapati and worshipped here, regaining his place among the gods — so the place is called Kuberapuri. Vishnu, in his boar (Varaha) form, is said to have worshipped the lord here with lotus flowers. The village name itself is explained by the belief that countless Shiva lingams lie beneath its soil. And it is told that when Sambandar came, he would not set foot on so sacred a ground, worshipping instead by rolling in circumambulation (angapradakshinam).
sections.festivals: The temple's foremost festival is the Aippasi Annabhishekam, in the Tamil month of Aippasi (October–November), when the lingam is bathed in cooked rice. The regular Shaiva observances of Maha Shivaratri, Pradosham and the Margazhi season are also kept, and the temple's Kubera association draws devotees seeking prosperity.
sections.experience: Sivapuram offers the pilgrim a temple whose quiet surface rests on a deep lore — a 'Kailasa on earth' said to hide countless lingams, where a god of wealth regained his place and the preserver himself came to worship. The darshan of Sivagurunathaswamy, close to the great temple town of Kumbakonam, rewards those who seek the layered sanctity of the delta.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Sivapuram is about 6 km east of Kumbakonam in Thanjavur district; Kumbakonam is the nearest rail head and town, with local buses and taxis to the village.
